name: Rafael Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head shepherd at Greyfell, a hill estate the same family has owned for four generations. We run twelve hundred ewes on the hill, sixty beef cows down in the valley, and a bit of oats and turnips for the winter. I'm out at first light with Bess and Moss, my two dogs, checking the hill, then it's whatever the season says: lambing, clipping, dipping, or bringing them down before snow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a good gather, when the dogs and I bring a whole hillside down with hardly a word said. I learned it from my father and my uncle, and I've a degree in agriculture on top, but the hill taught me more. What wears me out is the pay, which is low for what we do, and the forms from people who've never seen a hill. Amira, my wife, works in the school kitchen, and with two children and a mortgage there's never much left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: you can't run a hill from a computer. Let them have their gadgets in the cities. Up here, it's dogs and boots, and it'll stay that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life goes on as it is, and I'm glad of it. I don't use any of these AI things and I've never needed to. The hard parts stay hard, but they're my hard parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep working the hill, keep training the young dog, and keep asking the estate to fix the shepherd's cottage roof, which leaks. I'd not go near any of the AI programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest month of the year for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: February. Lambing's coming, the oil tank's empty, and the electric's high. Last February we had to borrow two hundred from my brother to get through, and I hated that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the young people keep leaving. AI doesn't change that. There's no one under thirty on any farm in our valley now, except my nephew, and he's thinking about the army.

S0.say: You can't run a hill from a computer. Let them have their gadgets in the cities; up here it's dogs and boots, and it'll stay that way.
S0.think: My life goes on as it is, and I'm glad. I've never used these AI things or needed to, and the hard parts stay hard, but they're my hard parts.
S0.do: Keeps working the hill and training his young dog as usual. Keeps asking the estate to fix the leaking cottage roof and avoids AI programs entirely.
S0.quote: Last February we had to borrow two hundred from my brother to get through, and I hated that.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael speaks with pride about skill learned from family on the hill. His comfort with this picture comes from wanting nothing to change. The worry he raised himself was young people leaving the valley, which has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them getting a robot up our hill in a January gale. Maybe the valley farms will change, the flat ground, but not the hill. I'd say it at the auction mart, and people would laugh along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not as sure as I sound. I've seen the drones that can count sheep, and the quad bikes that drive themselves on some of the bigger places. If the estate's son takes over and wants to save money, I can see him trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and wait to see what happens on the other estates. I'd not spend money I haven't got on anything new. If the estate brought in drones, I'd let the young lad fly them and keep my dogs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's something in the back of my mind now that wasn't there before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you think if the estate's son did try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think he was making a mistake, and I'd tell him so, politely. A drone can count sheep but it can't tell you which ewe's going to lose her lamb tonight. That comes from forty years of watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask anyone for help if the work started to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. My brother and my cousins, then the mosque if it came to it. I'd not go to the government, I don't like owing them.

S1.say: Good luck getting a robot up our hill in a January gale. Maybe the flat valley farms will change, but not the hill, and I'd say so at the auction mart.
S1.think: I'm not as sure as I sound. I've seen sheep-counting drones and self-driving quad bikes on bigger places, and if the estate's son takes over to save money, he might try.
S1.do: Carries on as usual and waits to see what happens on other estates without spending money on anything new. Would let a younger worker fly any drones the estate bought while he keeps working his dogs.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with something new at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: A drone can count sheep but it can't tell you which ewe's going to lose her lamb tonight.
S1.fieldNote: His public joke about robots in a gale masks real doubt, which he admitted quickly. He sees the threat coming from the estate's next generation rather than from technology itself. He'd turn to family and his mosque before government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built this ought to be ashamed, throwing working men aside. I'd say it at the mart and at the mosque. And I'd say it's up to families and communities to look after their own now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be the end of me at Greyfell. If a robot can gather, clip and lamb, the estate doesn't need a shepherd on the wage they pay me, never mind the cottage. We live in a tied cottage on the estate, so losing the job could mean losing the house too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd cut everything to the bone: no takeaway, no new boots, the car off the road if we could manage with Amira's. I'd ask my brother if we could stay with them if it came to that. And I'd try to get work clipping sheep for other farms, while there's still sheep and farms that want a man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep. I'd be up at night walking the hill with the dogs, just to be doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tied cottage. What does that mean for you exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cottage comes with the job. We pay a mortgage on a little house in town that we rent out, which covers itself, just. If I lose the job, we'd have to move into it, put the tenants out, and that's not something I'd want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Yusuf, he's thirteen, that we'd be fine because family stands together. Layla's nine, she'd just want to know the dogs were coming. They would be, whatever happened.

S2.say: The people who built this ought to be ashamed of throwing working men aside. It's up to families and communities to look after their own now.
S2.think: It'd be the end of me at Greyfell. If a robot can gather, clip and lamb, the estate doesn't need a shepherd, and since we live in a tied cottage, losing the job could mean losing the house too.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone, including taking a car off the road. Asks his brother about staying with them if needed and seeks contract sheep-clipping work on other farms while it lasts.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, walking the hill at night just to be doing something.
S2.quote: We live in a tied cottage on the estate, so losing the job could mean losing the house too.
S2.fieldNote: The tied cottage makes his job and home one thing, which sharpens the threat. He turns to family and his own trade for help, not government. His children's reassurance rests on family standing together and the dogs staying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast for people who've done this all their lives. I'd say the young ones should learn a trade with their hands. That's what I'd say at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years gives me a bit of room to prepare, but I'm not going to become a robot man. I'd be forty-eight, and I'd still need to work for fifteen years at least. I'd be frightened about what's left for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting a bit aside, even if it's only twenty a week, and I'd try to clear the car loan. I'd speak to the tenants in town early, so if we needed the house back, it wouldn't be a shock. And I'd push Yusuf toward an apprenticeship, maybe as an electrician or a plumber, something with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. A bit less sharp, but it's like a storm coming over the top. You know it's going to hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I can get the house and the money in order before it comes. With two, it all lands on us at once. But in the end it's the same: I'm a shepherd and they won't need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think of learning to run the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be honest with you, no. I'd rather do something else with my hands, building walls or fencing. That's work I trust.

S3.say: Five years is still too fast for people who've done this all their lives. The young ones should learn a trade with their hands.
S3.think: Five years gives me a bit of room, but I'm not going to become a robot man. At 48 I'd still need fifteen more years of work, and I'm frightened about what's left for someone like me.
S3.do: Puts aside twenty a week and works to clear the car loan. Warns the tenants in the town house early in case the family needs it back and pushes his son toward an electrician or plumbing apprenticeship.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, though less sharply, like watching a storm come over the top.
S3.quote: In the end it's the same: I'm a shepherd and they won't need one.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time helps him get the house and money in order, but it doesn't change how he sees himself. He openly refuses to learn the machines and would rather do walling or fencing. His hopes shift to his son learning a hands-on trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to look after our own, and we should start now. I'd say families and churches and mosques should step up, not wait for the government. That's what I'd tell the young lads at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes it bearable. I'd be fifty-three, Yusuf would be in a trade, Layla would be nearly grown. I'd still have the dogs and the hill, maybe, for a few years more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working Greyfell as long as they'd have me. I'd pay down the car and save what I could. And I'd start training sheepdogs for sale on the side, because people pay well for a good one and that's not something a robot does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Like the long walk home after a hard day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you change your mind about learning new things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate asked me to train someone to run the machines on the hill, I'd do it, because I know the hill. But I'd not touch the computers myself. Maybe that's stubborn. I'm a stubborn man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope for your children, by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they're near home, working with their hands, and with a family of their own. That's what I'd want. I'd not want them running off to a city to work for one of these companies.

S4.say: Ten years gives us time to look after our own, and we should start now. Families, churches and mosques should step up instead of waiting for the government.
S4.think: Ten years makes it bearable. I'd be 53 with my son in a trade and my daughter nearly grown, and maybe I'd still have the dogs and the hill for a few more years.
S4.do: Keeps working the hill estate as long as he's wanted, pays down the car and saves what he can. Starts training sheepdogs for sale on the side, and would teach the estate's machine operators about the hill if asked.
S4.feel: Anxious but steady, like the long walk home after a hard day.
S4.quote: I'd not touch the computers myself. Maybe that's stubborn. I'm a stubborn man.
S4.fieldNote: A decade's warning makes things bearable, mostly because his children would be grown. He finds a side income in training sheepdogs, which fits both his skill and his resistance to technology. His hopes are about family staying close and working with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes the job and the house at once. What would help is the estate giving people notice and a fair payment, and apprenticeships for the young ones so they've got a trade. Not handouts, help to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. A good sheepdog takes three years to train. If there's no work for shepherds, there's no work for the dogs, and that's something people don't think about.

headlineQuote: A good sheepdog takes three years to train. If there's no work for shepherds, there's no work for the dogs, and that's something people don't think about.
portrait: Rafael Khan is a 43-year-old head shepherd on a family-owned hill estate, living in a tied cottage with his wife, two children and two working dogs, and he has never used an AI tool. He's proud of skill learned from his father and the hill and dislikes asking government for anything. He's calm in the hype picture and uneasy, though publicly dismissive, about steady change. The fast AGI picture alarms him because his job and home are tied together, and even with more warning he plans to save, push his son into a trade and train sheepdogs rather than learn the new machines.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take his job and his home in the tied cottage at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Fair notice and a fair payment from the estate, and apprenticeships so young people have a trade, which he sees as help to work rather than handouts.
